You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

- id: 608ZZ
  od:
    measured: 21.22
    used: 22.0
    note: 608 OD is 22.000 -0.008; the video shows the bearing pinched at the jaw

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

I borrowed my friend's tripod, and I can't seem to find the part that connects the camera to the tripod. How hard would it be to 3D print it, both the flat part and the part that screws in? Just as a temporary thing until I find the real one. I know it's metal normally.

reasoning:
The user wants a camera-to-tripod quick release plate — the flat part (the QR plate that clamps into the tripod head) and the part that screws in (the 1/4"-20 screw that goes into the camera). They want it temporary, so PLA is fine.

Let me think about what's needed:

1. A tripod quick release plate. But wait — "the part that connects the camera to the tripod" — that could be:
   - The QR plate that slides into the tripod head's clamp
   - The 1/4"-20 bolt that screws into the camera's tripod socket

They said "both the flat part and the part that screws in". Hmm — actually on many tripod heads, the QR plate comes with an integrated 1/4"-20 screw that you turn (or via a hex) to attach the camera. So the "part that screws in" is the screw/bolt that goes into the camera.

But actually, the camera socket is a metal thread; screwing a PLA screw into it will destroy the plastic screw quickly. Better: use a real 1/4"-20 bolt. The hardware list includes "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (a 1/4"-20 nut) and "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt" (1/4"-20 bolt from a webcam monitor mount!). That's perfect — the salvaged webcam mount bolt is a 1/4"-20 bolt that can screw into the camera. We don't know its length/head shape. We could measure it.

So design:
- A PLA QR plate shaped to fit their tripod head's clamp, with a pocket/captive nut (the ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20 hex nut) or a slot for the salvaged webcam-mount-bolt, plus a hole through which the bolt screws into the camera.

Key unknowns that need measuring:
1. Their tripod head's QR clamp: slot width, length, any rails/grooves, the safety-latch geometry. This is the hard part. Many tripods use standard Manfrotto RC2 (35mm wide slot) or Arca-Swiss style (38mm wide), or screw-clamp. We need to measure their tripod head: slot width, slot length, rail geometry.
2. Camera bottom: location of the 1/4-20 socket relative to the plate, flatness of camera bottom, how deep the socket is, how much clearance needed around it (lens or battery door).
3. The salvaged webcam bolt: length, head type/diameter.

Turns available: at most 8. We should ask measurements efficiently. Each measure() call asks one thing. We can batch independent measure calls in one block. But the person has to answer; batching is allowed for independent calls. Let me plan:

Round 1 (batch):
- tripod head: QR slot width (inside width of the clamp slot)
- tripod head: QR slot length (how deep the clamp opens... actually the length of the slot the plate slides into / how long the clamp opening is)
- camera: diameter of the 1/4-20 socket recess (if any) and clearance around it
- webcam bolt: length

Actually measure() asks the person to measure one of their own things. They can measure the tripod head. Good.

But also whether the clamp is Arca or RC2 style: the profile of the slot (V-grooves?). We could ask them to measure width and length, and maybe describe. The measure tool returns what they measured or "can't". We can ask for width; if they say ~38mm it's Arca-ish, ~35 is Manfrotto RC2.

Also the bolt for the camera: the salvaged webcam-mount-bolt length — if it's short (like 10mm), fine for a camera (typical 1/4-20 socket depth ~6mm). If it's long, we need a nut pocket.

Also: does the tripod head clamp have a screw knob (screw-type Arca clamp) or lever? Doesn't matter much for the plate.

Also plate needs: anti-twist (camera body sits on the plate; a flange or rub pins to stop rotation). For temporary, maybe keep simple but include a ridge/lip around camera footprint? Cameras vary. Simpler: make the plate with the bolt through the center, and ask the user if they want anti-twist. Keep simple: temporary.

Material concerns: PLA screwing a metal nut into plastic: use a hex nut pocket (captive nut) — nut pocket with the nut pressed in, and the bolt threads through the nut into the camera. The plate experiences bending load from the camera weight cantilevered... actually the camera sits on the tripod head, load is compression through the plate. Fine for PLA.

Also the "flat part" — the QR plate must have a dovetail/side profile matching the clamp groove: Arca-style is a trapezoid 45° sides, 38-39mm wide top... For RC2 it's a plate with two ridges. Let's just measure the clamp and design a sliding dovetail plate accordingly.

Plan the measuring questions (batch in one turn, all independent):

Turn 1:
1. measure("tripod head clamp", "inside width of the slot the plate slides into") — Arca ~38-39mm, RC2 ~35mm.
2. measure("tripod head clamp", "inside length of the slot from the back stop to the front opening") 
3. measure("webcam mount bolt", "shank length (threads included)") — the bolt they have.
4. measure("camera bottom", "distance from the tripod socket centre to the front edge of the camera bottom")? Hmm, too many things. Maybe simpler: ask "diameter of the flat area around the tripod socket" for clearance. Actually many cameras have a recess around the socket; need depth clearance so plate is flat against camera. Let's ask: "camera, around the 1/4-20 socket: is the bottom flat, and how big is any raised bump or recess?" That's two things. The measure tool takes item+what as strings; the person answers. We can ask one dimension per call. Let's prioritize:

Essential measurements:
A. Clamp slot width (defines plate width).
B. Clamp slot length (max plate length, also where the stop is).
C. Webcam bolt usable length (defines stack height: plate + bolt head... wait, how is the bolt attached?).

How does the bolt attach to the plate? Options:
- Bolt head captive in a D-shaped slot (coin-slot style): bolt head sits in a slot, rotate to lock. Classic Manfrotto 200PL has a hex. Simpler: the bolt head sits in a hex pocket (captive) and threads into camera; you turn the whole plate? No — you turn the bolt with a coin or hex key.
- Simplest reliable: hex nut pocket in the plate underside? Wait geometry: plate sits on tripod; camera sits on top of plate; bolt goes from below through the plate up into the camera socket. The bolt head is under the plate (between plate bottom and tripod head?) No — the plate bottom sits in the clamp; there's no room below for the bolt head... Actually there IS room if the clamp's slot is open below (the plate rests on the clamp floor, bolt head would be between plate and floor — no room).

Standard design: the QR plate has the bolt integrated; the bolt's head is captive in the plate (recessed flush or slightly below), and you turn the bolt with a large coin-slot or a hex socket from... hmm, typically from the front edge (the plate has the screw sticking out the front, turned by hand or coin). Manfrotto 200PL-38: the bolt is fixed to the plate, its head is captive, and there's a hex/coin slot at the front? Actually the 200PL has a folding handle? No, the 200PL's screw is turned with a coin from the front edge... Let me recall: Manfrotto 200PL has a round hole at front center where you insert a coin or screwdriver to rotate the 1/4" screw. Yes.

Simplest for print: bolt head captive in a hex pocket from below (pocket open at the bottom of the plate, with a lip flange that holds the nut? no...).

Two clean options:

Option 1 (nut pocket from below + long bolt): Plate with a vertical through-hole. Under the plate... no room under the plate when mounted.

Option 2 (captive nut in the plate from the top face? no, camera sits on top).

Option 3: The nut is captured in the plate in a hex pocket that opens at the *front edge* of the plate? Hmm no.

Let's think again. Real QR plates: the screw head is captive within the plate body. The plate is maybe 8-12mm thick. The screw head sits in a hexagonal pocket (for hex head bolt) or a cylindrical pocket with a D-flat... For our salvaged webcam bolt: unknown head type. If it's a socket-head (probably, webcam mounts often use SHCS or a knurled head), head_d unknown, length unknown.

Alternative clean approach: use the ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20 hex nut + we need a bolt. The only 1/4-20 bolt available is the salvaged webcam-mount-bolt. So measure it.

Attachment: put a hex pocket in the plate's *side*? Odd. Let's do: pocket from the underside, and the plate has raised "feet"/flange... no.

Better: Make the bolt captive via a nut pocket that is open to the bottom but the plate sits on the clamp floor only on two rails (the sides of the clamp groove). I.e., plate underside is relieved in the middle where the bolt head is, leaving clearance above the clamp floor. Arca clamps: the clamp floor is flat; plate bottom flat. The bolt head would contact the floor and prevent seating — unless we relieve the underside so the bolt head is recessed above the seating plane... but then when the camera is tightened, the bolt head pulls up against the underside of the relief (a nut-like pocket). That works: a pocket in the underside, open downward, sized so the bolt head can slide in sideways, with a narrower slot constraining it. Then when you tighten the bolt (turning it with... how do you turn it?), the head pulls against the pocket ceiling. You turn the bolt via a coin slot or hex key from below — accessible because the pocket is open downward and the camera tightening happens while the plate is off... no wait, you tighten the bolt while the plate is attached to the camera, then slide the assembly into the clamp. The pocket faces down; after assembly, the pocket is covered by the clamp floor? No: the plate sits ON the clamp floor; the pocket is recessed INTO the plate, so its opening faces down toward the clamp floor, but the pocket interior is above the plate's seating surface. You can still access the pocket through its downward opening? The clamp floor is right there but there's no gap. Hmm, but you don't need to access it after assembly: you turn the bolt with a coin/hex from the top? No, camera is on top.

Standard solution: turn the bolt from the FRONT edge: the bolt extends forward beyond the plate front with a coin slot, or the plate has a front hole to reach the bolt head pocket. Manfrotto: the bolt head is in a captive pocket and there's a large coin slot in the front-center of the plate? Actually the 200PL's screw is operated by inserting a coin into a hole at the front of the plate that engages a slot in the screw head. Let me not overthink. 

Simplest robust: hex socket cap screw? We don't have one in 1/4-20 except the salvaged one (unknown head). 

Alternative: Use the salvaged bolt with a captive "nut" approach turned around: Put the bolt head in a pocket accessible from the FRONT of the plate: i.e., a horizontal pocket at the front face? Ugly.

Cleanest printable design that many DIY QR plates use: the plate has a through-hole; a 1/4-20 hex nut is captured in a hex pocket milled (printed) into the underside; the bolt comes from below through the nut; the bolt head (with coin slot or knurl) sits below the plate in a relieved area... The relief issue again.

Wait — actually in many Arca-style clamps, the clamp floor is NOT in contact with the plate's full underside; the plate's dovetail bottom face... no, the bottom face is flat and rests on the clamp floor.

Hmm, let me look at actual Manfrotto 200PL-38 design: Plate thickness ~10mm. The 1/4" screw: its head is captive in the plate; at the front end of the plate, the screw protrudes forward with a hex nut shape? No... The 200PL: the screw is at the center; you turn it with a coin inserted into a slot at the front? I recall the 200PL-38 has a circular hole on the front face through which you insert a screwdriver/coin. Actually I think the screw's head has a slot and the head is recessed into the plate's front region — the plate front has a circular hole aligned with the screw axis?? No.

Let me just design our own with the constraint "turn from the front": Bolt axis vertical (into camera). The bolt head pocket is a hex pocket open at the BOTTOM of the plate. Below the plate, when the plate is on the camera and you're tightening, the plate is in your hand — the bolt pocket is open downward and you can insert an Allen key or coin into the bolt head from below before sliding into the clamp? Yes! Sequence: 1) put bolt head into pocket from below (sideways slide-in), 2) flip plate over, screw into camera (turning the bolt with hex key from below — accessible), 3) slide assembly into tripod clamp. The pocket opening faces down; nothing blocks it because you're holding the assembly in air. Once in the clamp, the pocket faces the clamp floor — no access needed anymore. 

But wait: will the bolt head stay in the pocket? Design the pocket as: a wider hex recess (head slides in from below, rotating not needed) with a narrow "waist" slot through to the top hole — no wait, the bolt must pass through to the camera. Geometry: from bottom: hex pocket depth h_pocket; then a circular clearance hole (bolt shank d=6.35) through remaining plate thickness to the top face. The bolt head is captured by the pocket walls; the shank passes through the clearance hole. To load: insert shank through clearance hole from top? Head is bigger than clearance hole... Insert from bottom: push bolt up until head sits in hex pocket, shank protrudes out the top hole. Yes, that works if pocket depth ≥ head height. The head can't pull out downward because... it CAN pull out downward (nothing retains it once pocket opens down)! Need retention: pocket mouth slightly smaller than head across flats? Then head must be pushed in with rotation (like a twist-lock) — messy. Alternative: pocket mouth has a flange with a snap? For a temporary part, use a coin-slot retainer: a small "lid" over part of the pocket mouth leaving a slot for the shank, open at one side so the head slides in sideways, then a twist? 

Simplest: make the pocket mouth a "keyhole": wider channel sideways. E.g., pocket opens downward with a mouth; add two lips that leave a slot of width w < head_d... If mouth slot is narrower than head, head can't enter. Keyhole shape: a circular hole of diameter slightly less than head_d, connected to a side channel of width slightly more than head_d... The head enters through the side channel, slides to center, and the circular hole's overhang retains it. But the channel also opens to the plate edge? Then head could slide out the side — retain with a stop at channel end: head slides in from the plate's side edge (open), along a channel, stops at center, now circular recess above retains it... no, the recess is above (pocket ceiling). Let me re-think: pocket = hex recess in the underside. Mouth of pocket opens downward. To retain head: reduce the mouth to a slot narrower than the head across one axis but the head needs to get in. Keyhole from the edge: a slot from the plate's front edge? Hmm.

MUCH simpler alternative: don't capture the bolt head in the plate. Instead: the plate has a through-hole; the bolt goes through and threads into the camera; the ASME 1/4-20 hex NUT sits in a hex pocket in the plate's TOP face around the hole?? No wait. Flip it: bolt head on TOP, screwing DOWN into camera through the plate. Nut on the underside... but underside contacts clamp floor. 

Hmm OK what about: bolt head on top means the head sits between camera bottom and plate top — camera would rock on the head. No.

What about: don't use a separate bolt at all — the plate itself has the 1/4-20 thread printed in PLA and screws into the camera. The user asked exactly this: "both the flat part and the part that screws in" — they imagine a printed screw! A printed 1/4-20 screw thread in PLA WILL work into a metal socket temporarily, but it's weak; threads will deform after a few uses. The better answer: use the salvaged webcam bolt (real metal, right thread) + a printed captive arrangement, or print the "screw" part as a thumb-knob that grips the salvaged bolt. 

Actually, a neat approach: the "part that screws in" = a printed thumb knob that captures the salvaged webcam-mount bolt. The bolt threads into the camera; the printed knob has an internal hex pocket (or a split clamp) around the bolt head so you can turn the bolt by hand. And the "flat part" = the QR plate with a central clearance hole; the bolt passes through the plate into the camera, with its head... held by the knob from below. So the knob is BELOW the plate — again the clamp floor interference!

Unless... the knob sits IN a recess in the plate's underside: i.e., the plate's underside has a circular relief pocket; the knob (printed) sits in that pocket; the bolt passes through the knob. The knob's outer diameter is captured by the pocket (pocket depth > knob thickness? then knob rotates freely inside but is retained vertically). The knob has a coin-slot or hex bore for the bolt head? If bolt head is captive in the knob's pocket (bolt head in knob, knob in plate pocket, shank through plate hole into camera). Tighten by turning the knob (hand grip? knob is flush in the plate...).

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider the clamp geometry. Many Arca clamps: the opening at the front is a wide slot; the plate slides in sideways. The clamp floor... Actually you know what, many plates are NOT flush with clamp floor; the clamp grips the plate's sides. The plate's bottom face sits on the floor. The plate thickness is free above: top face is where the camera sits. So all the mechanism must be WITHIN the plate thickness (10-15mm) or recessed into the underside only in areas where the clamp floor has relief... unknowable.

Alternatively, front-access: Make the plate LONGER at the front (like Manfrotto), with the bolt head pocket near the front? No, the bolt must be at the camera socket location, which is central-ish on the plate.

OK here's another classic DIY solution (I've seen many on printables): The QR plate has a hex nut captured in a hex pocket open at the plate's FRONT EDGE (horizontally), and the bolt is inserted from the front horizontally?? No...

Let me search memory: "Printables quick release plate 1/4-20 captive nut" — designs typically: plate with vertical hex pocket from the underside; the pocket is covered by a printed "cap" piece screwed/pressed, or the nut is inserted with a snap-fit lip; the bolt goes up through the nut; bolt head below plate with a recess... The stack: clamp floor — [bolt head in its own recess within clamp floor? no].

Honestly, maybe simplest and most robust: THUMB SCREW approach with the bolt head BELOW the plate and accept that the plate's underside around the bolt head is relieved, and the clamp floor has clearance because... we can measure the clamp! We're going to measure the clamp slot anyway. Ask: "when a plate sits in the slot, is there any clearance below the plate / how deep is the slot's floor relief?" Too complicated for them to measure.

Cleanest actually-workable design given constraints (temporary use):

Design: Two printed parts.
1. QR plate (dovetail to match their clamp, width measured). Central area: a hex pocket from the TOP face, covered? No—camera needs flat top.

Hmm, what if the nut goes in a pocket that opens to the TOP, and the camera's bottom has a recess around the socket? Cameras often have a slight recess. No, unreliable.

What if we make the plate with the nut pocket opening at the bottom, and the bolt head pocket ALSO at the bottom, and simply RELIEVE the plate's underside locally so the bolt head sits ~2mm above the plate's bottom plane... that doesn't help: the bolt head still protrudes below into the space between plate underside plane and clamp floor?
